fact: Often the first bird to sing in the morning, sometimes starting well before sunrise.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Lawns, parks, gardens and woodland edges, often running across grass and stopping to look down.
listen: A rich, rising and falling carol, often remembered as "cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio."

fact: Unlike most songbirds, the female sings too, sometimes while sitting on the nest.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Thickets, gardens and woodland edges; often at feeders, early and late in the day.
listen: Loud, clear whistles that slur down and up, like "birdie, birdie, birdie" or "cheer, cheer, cheer."

fact: The more "dee" notes at the end of its call, the bigger the threat it has spotted.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Mixed and leafy woods, and backyards with trees, usually in small busy flocks.
listen: A sweet two-note whistle, "fee-bee," and the scolding "chick-a-dee-dee-dee."

fact: It can sing two notes at once, harmonizing with itself using the two sides of its voice box.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: The shady floor of mature leafy forests in summer.
listen: Flute-like phrases, often "ee-oh-lay," each ending in a soft, buzzy trill.

fact: Each male knows several different songs and repeats one many times before switching.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Shrubby fields, marsh edges and yards, singing from a low, open perch.
listen: A few clear notes, then a jumble and a trill, remembered as "Maids, maids, maids, put on your tea kettle."

fact: It weighs less than an ounce, yet its song carries across a whole neighborhood.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Tangles, brush piles and wooded backyards, usually low down and hard to see.
listen: A loud, rolling "teakettle, teakettle, teakettle."

fact: Its clear whistled song is often remembered as "Oh-sweet-Canada-Canada-Canada."
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Forest undergrowth in summer; brushy thickets and backyards in winter.
listen: A thin, pure whistle, "Oh-sweet-Canada-Canada-Canada."

fact: Every song opens with one long clear note, and each new song starts at a different pitch.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Conifer and mixed forests in summer; thickets in winter, often flicking its reddish tail.
listen: One long, clear note, then a spiral of airy flute notes; each song starts at a new pitch.

fact: It can imitate the scream of a Red-shouldered Hawk, possibly to warn other jays or scare off rivals.
size: Between a robin and a crow
habitat: Oak woods, parks and suburbs, often in noisy family groups.
listen: A loud, harsh "jay! jay!", soft bell-like notes, and hawk imitations.

fact: Its wings make a sharp whistling sound when it takes off, a built-in alarm for the rest of the flock.
size: Between a robin and a crow
habitat: Open country, farmland and suburbs; often on wires and at feeders.
listen: A soft, sad "coo-OO-oo, oo, oo."

fact: A male can learn around 200 songs, and unmated males often keep singing all night.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Towns, parks and open ground with shrubs, singing from rooftops and treetops.
listen: A long run of borrowed phrases, each repeated several times before it switches.

fact: Males stuff sticks into several nest cavities, and the female picks which one to finish.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Yards, parks and woodland edges, often in nest boxes.
listen: A fast, bubbly cascade of notes that tumbles down the scale.

fact: It lines its nest with hair, sometimes plucked straight from a living animal.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Leafy woods and backyards with big trees; a regular at feeders.
listen: A clear, repeated whistle, "peter-peter-peter."

fact: It nests late in summer, waiting until thistles and milkweed have soft down for the nest.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Weedy fields, roadsides and feeders, in bouncing, roller-coaster flight.
listen: A twittering song, and a flight call like "po-ta-to-chip" with each dip.

fact: A single male may have several females nesting in the patch of marsh he defends.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Marshes, wet ditches and fields, males calling from cattails.
listen: A gurgling "conk-la-ree!" that ends in a trill.

fact: There is no blue pigment in its feathers: the color comes from how their structure scatters light.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Open fields and meadows with scattered trees, fence lines and nest boxes.
listen: A soft, warbling "tu-a-wee" or "cheer, cheerful charmer."

fact: The female weaves a hanging pouch of a nest from plant fibers, hair and string.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Open woods, riversides and tall shade trees in parks and towns.
listen: Rich, flute-like whistled phrases, a little different from bird to bird.

fact: Its song is often described as a robin that has taken voice lessons.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Leafy forest edges and wooded yards in summer.
listen: A sweet, robin-like caroling song, and a sharp "eek" call like a squeaky sneaker.

fact: One male was counted singing more than 20,000 songs in a single day.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: High in the leafy canopy of eastern forests in summer.
listen: Short phrases with pauses, over and over: "Here I am. Where are you? Over here."

fact: Its song is remembered as "drink-your-tea!", the last note a quick trill.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Brushy thickets and forest edges, scratching noisily in dead leaves.
listen: "Drink-your-tea!", and a rising "chwee?" call.

fact: It is named for its mewing call, which sounds remarkably like a cat.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Dense shrubs, hedges and tangled edges, often heard before seen.
listen: A long, rambling jumble of squeaks and whistles, with a cat-like "mew" call.

fact: It has been recorded with more than 1,100 different song types, usually sung in pairs.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Thickets, hedgerows and brushy edges, usually low down.
listen: Loud, varied phrases, usually sung in pairs: "plant-a-seed, plant-a-seed."

fact: It is the state bird of six US states, more than almost any other bird.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Grasslands, prairies and farm fields, singing from fence posts.
listen: A bubbling, flute-like song that tumbles down at the end.

fact: Its flute-like song spirals upward, each phrase climbing higher than the last.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Dense, damp forests in summer; it migrates through woods and parks.
listen: Breezy, flute-like phrases that spiral upward.

fact: Its song spirals downward, sounding like it is being sung inside a metal pipe.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Damp leafy forests with thick undergrowth.
listen: A breezy song that spirals downward, "veer, veer, veer."

fact: It is named for its domed nest on the forest floor, shaped like an old outdoor oven.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: The floor of mature leafy forests, walking rather than hopping.
listen: "Teacher, teacher, TEACHER," getting louder as it goes.

fact: Its bright song is often remembered as "sweet, sweet, sweet, I'm so sweet."
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Willows, wet thickets and shrubby edges near water.
listen: Bright and quick: "sweet, sweet, sweet, I'm so sweet."

fact: The masked male sings a rolling "witchety-witchety-witchety" from marshes and wet fields.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Marshes, wet fields and dense low growth.
listen: A rolling "witchety-witchety-witchety."

fact: It migrates at night and learns to steer by the stars, as experiments in a planetarium showed.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Brushy edges, roadsides and old fields, singing from wires and treetops.
listen: Bright paired notes: "what! what! where? where? see it! see it!"

fact: It used to line its nest with horsehair so often that it was nicknamed the hair bird.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Open woods, parks and lawns with scattered trees.
listen: A long, dry trill on one pitch, like a tiny sewing machine.

fact: Often called the snowbird, because it shows up at feeders across much of the US as winter arrives.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Conifer forests in summer; yards and feeders in winter, flashing white tail edges.
listen: A musical trill on one pitch, and sharp ticking calls.

fact: A male's red comes from pigments in his food, and females tend to prefer the reddest males.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Towns, farms and backyard feeders.
listen: A long, cheerful warble that often ends in a buzzy note.

fact: It sings its own name, and was the first bird ever banded in North America, by Audubon in 1804.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Near water, under bridges and the eaves of buildings, wagging its tail.
listen: A raspy "fee-bee," its own name.

fact: Its song has local dialects, so birds a few miles apart can sound noticeably different.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Brushy areas and weedy fields, especially in winter.
listen: A clear whistle followed by buzzy notes and a trill, in a local dialect.

fact: The red on the male's face likely comes from pigments in the insects it eats.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Open conifer and mixed forests in the West.
listen: Like a hoarse American Robin, short burry phrases.

fact: Its call is remembered as "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?"
size: About the size of a crow
habitat: Mature forests and wooded swamps, often near water.
listen: "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?"

fact: It sings nearly all year, and near street lights it will often sing at night.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Gardens, parks and woodland, often following gardeners for worms.
listen: A wistful, liquid warbling, sung nearly all year.

fact: Its mellow, flute-like song is a classic sound of dawn and dusk, often delivered from a rooftop.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Gardens, parks and woods, singing from rooftops and treetops at dawn and dusk.
listen: Slow, mellow, flute-like phrases.

fact: It repeats each phrase two or three times before moving on to the next.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Gardens, parks and woods with undergrowth.
listen: Bold phrases, each repeated two or three times.

fact: One of the smallest birds in Europe, it packs dozens of notes into a few seconds of song.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Undergrowth, gardens and woodland, low and mouse-like.
listen: A startlingly loud, fast song packed with trills.

fact: Chaffinches have regional dialects: birds a few valleys apart sing slightly different songs.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Woods, parks and gardens across Europe.
listen: A descending rattle of notes that ends in a flourish.

fact: Its rich warbling earned it the nickname "northern nightingale."
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Woodland and gardens with plenty of shrubs.
listen: A rich, fluty warble that bursts out of thick cover.
